paragraphs: The Type 31 was designed to be affordable, and that shows in the hull: a straightforward flared bow, a large superstructure block and a flight deck aft, without the faceted stealth shaping that drives cost up on larger frigates. In Polish service the ship carries its own pennant and markings, and the model keeps the mast array, the gun mount and the boat davits.
The mesh is efficient at 192,933 polygons and 205,945 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, which suits a vessel that usually appears at sea rather than at close quarters.

At $199 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits naval and defence visualisation, news and documentary graphics, shipbuilding and procurement presentation, and games. On sale since 2025, kept to real-world scale for correct placement in a formation.

A modern destroyer is built around its radar. The four fixed panels on the superstructure fix the shape of the deckhouse, the vertical launch cells set the deck layout fore and aft, and the whole hull is angled to reduce radar return. This model carries that arrangement along with the gun mount, the mast array and the helicopter deck.
The mesh is 357,903 polygons and 388,741 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, built to StemCell specification so it works in a real-time engine as well as an offline render.

This page is unusually deep: a Type 055 variant at $199, versions paired with a Harbin helicopter at $249, and builds with a transport helicopter on the pad at $289. Aimed at naval and defence visualisation, news graphics, documentary work and games.

A film set reads as a film set because of the equipment scattered around it: a camera on a tripod, a monitor cart, light stands, a slate, cases and cable runs, with someone in a director's chair in the middle of it. A single camera model cannot produce that impression. This collection provides the figure and the kit together, which is what a production scene actually needs.
Buying the equipment as a set keeps the scale and the finish consistent across the whole scene, which is the detail that gives away a set dressed from separate sources.

At $199 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits film and television production visualisation, studio and rental company marketing, media education material, behind-the-scenes illustration and games. On sale since 2025.

Stamford Bridge is a stadium built into a tight west London site, and that constraint gives it its character: four stands of different heights and depths, pressed hard against the streets around them, with none of the symmetry of a purpose-built bowl. Any model that regularises those stands stops being Stamford Bridge and becomes a generic ground.

This is by a wide margin one of the heaviest assets in the catalogue at 36,423,673 polygons and 35,263,035 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs. Every seat is geometry rather than a texture, which is why the stands read correctly from the pitch, from the stands and from the air.

At $189 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits sports broadcast graphics, club and sponsorship presentation, architectural and venue visualisation, football games and print. On sale since 2025.

A dwarf is a rigging problem before it is an art problem. Short limbs, a broad torso and heavy armour mean the shoulders and hips deform in ways a human proportion never has to handle, and a rig that works on a standard figure will pinch and collapse here. This character arrives rigged with that already solved, along with the braided beard that most dwarf models get wrong.

The mesh is 85,995 polygons and 89,405 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs - a game-appropriate budget that leaves room for the armour plates and the beard without pushing the figure out of real-time range.

Two more rigged builds share this page at the same $189, prepared for Cinema 4D and for Maya. Aimed at games, fantasy film and television, previsualisation, tabletop and illustration work. On sale since 2025.

A mobile batching plant is a factory that folds onto a trailer. Aggregate bins, a conveyor, a cement silo, a weighing hopper and the mixer itself all have to be there, arranged so material flows downhill from bin to truck. That flow is what makes the machine legible to anyone who has worked around one, and a plant modelled without it reads as a random stack of hoppers.

The mesh is 687,836 polygons and 750,650 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 18 texture maps - 12 at 4096x4096, 4 at 2048x2048 and 2 at 1024x1024. The textures carry the cement dust and the rust that this equipment wears within weeks.
At $189 it suits construction and infrastructure visualisation, equipment marketing and catalogues, engineering and training material, site scenes and games. On sale since 2019.

The Coronado bridge is remembered for its curve. It sweeps through a long arc rather than running straight across the bay, partly to gain the height needed for ships to pass underneath, and that curve is what makes it photograph the way it does. A straight-span model of it would be recognisably wrong from the first frame.

The mesh runs 698,380 polygons and 727,194 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 37 texture maps at 4096x4096. Thirty-seven maps is an unusual count and it is what a structure this long needs: concrete weathering and deck markings that never visibly repeat.
At $179 it suits city and infrastructure visualisation, civil engineering presentation, travel and tourism material, film and television establishing shots, and games. On sale since 2018.

A freight train is not a locomotive, it is a consist. This build supplies both: the road unit in CSX colours plus the cars behind it, which is what lets a scene show a train rather than an engine parked on a rail. The ES44AC carries the flared radiator section at the rear that identifies the model, and the model keeps the walkways, handrails and truck castings.

It is a heavy asset at 3,111,707 polygons and 3,194,707 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, which is what a multi-vehicle consist costs when every unit is built to the same standard rather than the cars being simplified.
At $179 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits rail and logistics visualisation, industrial and infrastructure renders, simulator projects, film and television, and games. On sale since 2024.

The S-92 is the machine that flies crews to offshore platforms, and that mission shapes it: a large cabin with airline-style seating, a retractable gear, flotation gear in the sponsons and a rear ramp for cargo. It is a heavy helicopter that spends its life over water, and the model keeps the sponsons, the ramp and the antenna array that go with the role.

The mesh is 309,578 polygons and 338,116 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 17 texture maps at 4096x4096, which is what an operator livery needs over a fuselage this size.

A rigged build sits on this page at $229 for when the rotors turn and the gear retracts. The static model at $179 covers offshore energy visualisation, search and rescue presentation, corporate and government aviation marketing, film and television, and games. Built to StemCell specification, on sale since 2020.

This is two machines on one chassis: a drum mixer keeping the concrete turning and a placing boom to put it where it is needed. Combining them saves a second truck on a tight site, and it gives the vehicle a distinctive silhouette - a folded boom lying over a rotating drum. The model carries the boom sections, the outriggers, the drum ribs and the discharge chute.

The mesh runs 708,485 polygons and 764,247 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the density in the boom joints and the drum drive, which are the parts a camera on a construction site actually lands on.

At $169 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits construction and infrastructure visualisation, equipment marketing and catalogues, site scenes, safety and training material, and games. On sale since 2025.

The 737-800 is the aircraft that built the European low cost model, and Ryanair operates more of them than anyone. The scheme is deliberately simple - white fuselage, blue belly, yellow harp on the tail - which leaves nowhere for a stretched stencil or a misplaced door outline to hide. The model carries the winglets, the flap track fairings and the engine nacelle flats.
The mesh is 738,707 polygons and 764,152 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 7 texture maps at 4096x4096.

A rigged build sits on this page at $199 for when the gear retracts or the control surfaces move. The static model at $149 covers airline marketing, airport visualisation, aviation journalism, film and television, and games. On sale since 2017.

A wrapped figure is a costume problem more than an anatomy one. The bandages have to overlap unevenly, hang loose where they have come undone and pull tight across the ribs and limbs, and the body underneath has to show through in the gaps. Modelled as a smooth figure with a bandage texture, it reads as a painted statue.

The mesh is deliberately light at 4,328 polygons and 4,319 vertices in quads and tris. The UVs overlap, a sound economy on a subject made of repeated wrapping, and the low weight suits a figure that usually appears in groups.

At $149 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits horror games and film, Halloween and seasonal advertising, haunted attraction and event design, archaeology and museum material, and illustration. On sale since 2026.

The Frecciarossa 1000 is one of the fastest trains in regular service in Europe, and it looks the part: a long tapered nose, a pantograph recess in the roof and a body profile drawn entirely by aerodynamics. The red and silver livery runs the length of the set, and any break in that line is immediately visible, which puts real demands on the surfacing.

The mesh runs 1,745,086 polygons and 961,981 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs. The vertex count sitting below the polygon count is normal on long smooth panels sharing edges, and it keeps a set this size manageable.

This page also carries a blue variant at $149, an ETR1000 locomotive build at $129 and a modern blue locomotive at $99. Aimed at rail marketing and infrastructure visualisation, travel advertising, news graphics, simulators and games. On sale since 2023.

Zvezda is the module that made the station habitable: life support, crew quarters, the galley and the engines that keep the whole assembly in orbit. Externally it is a cylinder covered in hardware - solar arrays, antennas, handrails, docking targets and thermal blankets - and that clutter is what makes it read as a spacecraft rather than as a tube.

The mesh is 339,190 polygons and 384,151 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 10 texture maps at 4096x4096. The texture work carries the blanket quilting and the sun-faded panels that a module in orbit for decades actually shows.
At $149 and built to StemCell specification, it suits space industry visualisation, documentary and news graphics, museum and education material, film and television, and games. On sale since 2021.
